newsitem.title: USA: Democrats caution White House on budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Democrats caution White House on budget deal.

text.p: House Democrats warned senior White House officials Tuesday against accepting the Republican offer on taxes and spending cuts, raising doubts of a quick budget deal.

In a closed door meeting with White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles and other top officials, Democrats said they could not agree to a $100 billion net tax cut by 2002 and had deep concerns about the spending cuts.

House Democratic aides said lawmakers showed a mixed reaction to the White House's continued efforts to negotiate a budget deal with Republicans. Some urged the administration to carry on with closed door bargaining sessions, and others urged that Republicans be forced to present their own budget to the public, the aides said.
There has been no announcement of a resumption of formal budget negotiations between the White House and Congress.

Earlier in the day Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, Republican of Mississippi, said a budget agreement could be worked out in 24 hours. But the prediction was not endorsed by House Majority Leader Dick Armey, Republican of Texas, who said it could take months for the process to be completed.

The annual budget serves as a blueprint for further legislation to enact the spending cuts and tax cuts it outlines. That process frequently takes until the start of the new fiscal year, Oct. 1, or beyond. This year both the White House and Republican leaders in Congress have said they aim to balance the budget by the year 2002.

Miller told reporters he was dismayed by the Republican tax cut offer because it has been projected to balloon to $250 billion over the next five year perior through 2007, meaning it will make the deficit worse in those years.
"You find yourself in a straitjacket for the next decade trying to get rid of that (tax cut) problem," he said.

Republicans offered to accept $125 billion in Medicare spending cuts but were still above the $100 billion limit set by the White House for the five years. The two sides were now $75 billion apart on the size of spending cuts in domestic programmes other than mandatory benefits payments.

Republicans have told the White House they want a gross tax cut of $150 billion over five years and would allow no more than $50 billion in tax increases to pay for it. Clinton has proposed $98 billion in tax cuts with $76 billion in tax increases to pay for it for a net cut of about $22 billion through 2002.
"It is hard to find any of it that is good," Representative Jim McDermott of Washington said of the Republican offer.
Bowles told reporters that a wide range of views were expressed in the meeting. "These viewpoints were expressed with real passion," he said.
Office of Management and Budget director Frank Raines, White House congressional liason John Hilley and Economic adviser Gene Sperling also spoke to the Democrats.

White House officials had met Senate Democrats earlier in the day. Sen. Kent Conrad of North Dakota said they were also concerned that large tax cuts would erode the gains made on the deficit. Whatever the outcome of the private budget negotiations, eventually the plan must be brought out in public and must please a majority if it is to pass, he said.
"It isn't a matter of a few people in a room. It has got to pass Congress," Conrad said.
